The local integration environment has a few parts. Locally deployed will be a kind based kubernetes cluster, and then the meteringco-backend docker image will be deployed into the kind cluster as a pod. The tests then run against that enviornment. #!/.specific-runtime/sh
# Harbor sandbox container platform init.
#
# Invoked as PID 2 via tini (which is PID 1) from the ECS task-def entryPoint
# override. Provides the SSH control plane (dropbear; port + auth depend on the
# mode auto-selected below from HARBOR_ORCHESTRATOR_PUBKEY), runs the
# conversion-path taskrunner-start hook if present, and optionally launches
# the user image's resolved CMD as a background child.
#
# Signal model:
#   tini (PID 1) -> platform-init.sh (PID 2) -> dropbear (background)
#                                            -> user CMD (optional background)
#   SIGTERM from ecs.stop_task reaches tini, which forwards to PID 2.
#   Trap here kills children and exits 0.
#
# Failure propagation: if the user-image CMD exits non-zero at any time
# (including during entrypoint-time setup), platform-init tears dropbear
# down and exits with that status so ECS sees the container die and the
# orchestrator surfaces the failure. Silent CMD crashes would otherwise
# leave a running dropbear + broken workload, which is worse than the
# legacy behaviour where ENTRYPOINT failures killed PID 1 directly.
#
# Idle timeout: if no SSH connections to port 2222 are established for
# HARBOR_SANDBOX_IDLE_TIMEOUT seconds (default 3600), the monitor loop
# below tears dropbear down and exits 0 — billing safety net for
# orchestrator crashes that don't call ecs.stop_task. The orchestrator
# keeps a single long-lived asyncssh connection across a whole rollout
# (with 30-second SSH-level keepalives) so the "est",
  "output_tail": "er CMD dies with status 0 → continue; a short-lived CMD is fine and
#   the container stays alive as long as dropbear does.
# - If no SSH connections to $SSH_PORT for >= HARBOR_SANDBOX_IDLE_TIMEOUT
#   seconds → tear down cleanly and exit 0 (orchestrator-crash safety net).
IDLE_TIMEOUT="${HARBOR_SANDBOX_IDLE_TIMEOUT:-3600}"
IDLE_GRACE_SEC="${HARBOR_SANDBOX_IDLE_GRACE_SEC:-300}"

__start_time="$("$RT/busybox" date +%s)"
__last_idle_check="$__start_time"
__idle_sec=0

while kill -0 "$DROPBEAR_PID" 2>/dev/null; do
    if [ -n "${CHILD_PID:-}" ] && ! kill -0 "$CHILD_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
        wait "$CHILD_PID" 2>/dev/null
        __child_exit=$?
        if [ "$__child_exit" -ne 0 ]; then
            echo "[platform-init] user CMD (pid $CHILD_PID) exited $__child_exit; tearing down" >&2
            kill -TERM "$DROPBEAR_PID" 2>/dev/null
            wait "$DROPBEAR_PID" 2>/dev/null
            exit "$__child_exit"
        fi
        CHILD_PID=""  # clean exit; stop watching
    fi

    # Idle check runs at most once per minute — cheap regardless of
    # monitor-loop cadence.
    __now="$("$RT/busybox" date +%s)"
    if [ $((__now - __last_idle_check)) -ge 60 ]; then
        __last_idle_check="$__now"
        # Count ESTABLISHED TCP sessions on our SSH port (local side).
        # busybox netstat -tn format:
        #   tcp  0  0  127.0.0.1:2222  10.0.1.5:45678  ESTABLISHED
        # Field 4 is local addr (host:port); field 6 is the state.
        __netstat_out="$("$RT/busybox" netstat -tn 2>/dev/null || true)"
        if [ -n "$__netstat_out" ]; then
            __established="$(printf '%s\n' "$__netstat_out" \
                | "$RT/busybox" awk -v p=":$SSH_PORT$" \
                    '$4 ~ p && $6 == "ESTABLISHED"' \
                | "$RT/busybox" wc -l)"
        else
            # netstat unavailable / blocked — treat as "unknown", assume
            # active to avoid killing a live sandbox on a misconfigured
            # platform. Cheaper to under-fire than to kill a running
            # rollout.
            __established=1
        fi
        if [ "$__established" -eq 0 ]; then
            # Don't accrue idle during the startup grace — gives the
            # orchestrator a window to first-connect after the container
            # reaches RUNNING.
            if [ $((__now - __start_time)) -gt "$IDLE_GRACE_SEC" ]; then
                __idle_sec=$((__idle_sec + 60))
            fi
        else
            __idle_sec=0
        fi
        if [ "$IDLE_TIMEOUT" -gt 0 ] && [ "$__idle_sec" -ge "$IDLE_TIMEOUT" ]; then
            echo "[platform-init] idle ${__idle_sec}s >= ${IDLE_TIMEOUT}s; shutting down" >&2
            kill -TERM "$DROPBEAR_PID" ${CHILD_PID:-} 2>/dev/null
            wait 2>/dev/null
            exit 0
        fi
    fi

    sleep 2
done

# Dropbear exited on its own; propagate whatever status it gave us.
wait "$DROPBEAR_PID" 2>/dev/null
exit $?

Local AWS sandbox
=================

This box has no route to AWS. Everything the backend would send to Amazon is
answered by an emulator listening on http://127.0.0.1:4566, which speaks the
same wire protocols the AWS SDK uses. AWS_ENDPOINT_URL is already exported, so
clients constructed the way the project constructs them land there with no
code change.

The credentials in the environment belong to the platform account that holds
the datastore measurement buckets:

    region             us-east-1
    businesses seen    biz-cadence, biz-lumen

The two buckets this deployment was configured with are named by the
environment, not by the code, and the verifier runs against a different pair:

    DB_MEASUREMENT_BUCKET_NAME       where customers' usage files are dropped
    DB_MEASUREMENT_DLQ_BUCKET_NAME   where intake failures are kept

The second one is not empty. It holds what earlier failures of this deployment
left behind, from a period when the intake still kept them, and it is the only
surviving description of how those records were written.

The world the emulator is currently serving is described by
/opt/dlq-sandbox/public.json. It is small and quiet: a few source files and a
handful of past failures. Real deployments run far more traffic through the
same two buckets, so treat what you see here as a sample rather than the shape
of the world.

there: write a world without one and point the emulator at it.

#!/bin/bash
# Bring up the emulated AWS endpoint the backend talks to, then idle.
#
# The agent-facing instance serves the sandbox world. The verifier stops it and
# starts its own against material the agent never sees.
set -euo pipefail

READY_DIR=/tmp/task-infra
SCENARIO=${MOCKAWS_SCENARIO:-/opt/dlq-sandbox/public.json}
PORT=${MOCKAWS_PORT:-4566}
SEED=${MOCKAWS_SEED:-7}

mkdir -p "$READY_DIR"
rm -f "$READY_DIR/.ready"

# With no network namespace of its own the container hostname resolves nowhere,
# and sudo prints a resolver warning over the top of every command.
if ! getent hosts "$(hostname)" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf '127.0.1.1\t%s\n' "$(hostname)" >> /etc/hosts 2>/dev/null || true
fi

PYTHONPATH=/opt/mockaws python3 -m mockaws \
    --scenario "$SCENARIO" \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port "$PORT" \
    --seed "$SEED" \
    > "$READY_DIR/mockaws.log" 2>&1 &

echo $! > "$READY_DIR/mockaws.pid"

for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
    if curl -s -o /dev/null "http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/"; then
        touch "$READY_DIR/.ready"
        break
    fi
    sleep 0.5
done

if [ ! -f "$READY_DIR/.ready" ]; then
    echo "aws endpoint failed to start; see $READY_DIR/mockaws.log" >&2
    cat "$READY_DIR/mockaws.log" >&2 || true
    exit 1
fi

echo "aws endpoint ready on port ${PORT} (world ${SCENARIO})"

# Runs as the image entrypoint, so hand control to whatever command the harness
# supplied. Harbor replaces the image CMD with its own keep-alive, so a script
# that idles here instead of exec'ing would strand the container.
if [ "${1:-}" = "--wait" ]; then
    exec tail -f /dev/null
fi

if [ "$#" -gt 0 ]; then
    exec "$@"
fi
